clue.text: Maria or Dud left describing heraldry

indicators.note: A dud is a thing that does not work as it should, so the letters beside it will not work in the order given.

parts.note: anagram fodder, seven letters
l = left, the eighth letter joining the fodder

explanation.surface: Maria and Dud walking out of the room, still talking about coats of arms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dud' sits beside Maria like a second nickname and is the instruction instead. Armorial bearings are the formal name for a coat of arms, so the definition is an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Armorial is the adjective for anything to do with coats of arms - armorial bearings, an armorial shield - which is the business of heraldry.

clue.text: Alan's smashed up about the nose

indicators.note: Smashing something up breaks it into pieces, and pieces can be put back in any order at all.

parts.note: anagram fodder, five letters with the apostrophe counting for nothing

explanation.surface: Alan has come off worse in a brawl and taken most of the damage around his face.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition wants a describing word, not a part of the body: a nasal spray, a nasal voice. A possessive is a gift to a setter, since 's adds a letter and hides the join.
explanation.definitionFit: Nasal means of or near the nose - nasal passages, a nasal twang - so anything about the nose is nasal.

clue.text: Test purity of tea? Almost unknown

indicators.note: almost means not quite all of the tea's name, so its final letter is dropped

parts.note: Assam is a strong black tea from north-east India
y is an unknown quantity in algebra

explanation.surface: Someone checks whether a cup of tea is pure, almost a mystery.
explanation.walkthrough: ASSAM loses its last letter to give ASSA, then Y joins it. 'Test purity of' reads as a whole verb phrase, which is how an assayer tests metal.
explanation.definitionFit: To assay a metal or ore is to analyse it chemically for its content and quality.

clue.text: Dishing out for a lively party

indicators.note: Out here means out of order, an instruction that the letters beside it are not standing where they belong.

parts.note: anagram fodder, seven letters

explanation.surface: Food being served up in quantity at somebody's celebration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dishing out' reads as one phrase, which is the disguise: the verb is the fodder and its little particle is the instruction. A shindig is the sort of party where the furniture gets moved back.
explanation.definitionFit: A shindig is a noisy, cheerful party or dance, a word that carries the racket and the crowd along with it.

clue.text: German man — he has luxury car

parts.note: the pronoun taken as it stands
RR is the badge of Rolls-Royce, the byword for a luxury car

explanation.surface: A gentleman in Germany who has a Rolls-Royce on the drive.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash does the work of a colon: the definition stops before it and the building starts after. Herr is the German equivalent of Mr, the title on the envelope.
explanation.definitionFit: German uses Herr where English uses Mr, the title that goes in front of a man's name in that country.

indicators.note: Odds are the odd-numbered ones, so the first, third, fifth, seventh and ninth letters are taken and the rest dropped.

parts.note: the odd-numbered letters of SPYTRAINAT, read straight through the word breaks

explanation.surface: Agents being trained up somewhere rural, with the trainers in disagreement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At odds' pulls hard as a single phrase and the setter has split it down the middle: 'at' is the last of the letters to be mined and only 'odds' is the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Syria is a country on the eastern Mediterranean, its capital Damascus.

parts.note: to saddle someone with a job is to burden them with it
the stern of a boat is its back end

explanation.surface: A stern-looking pig being loaded up with something heavy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stern' is the back of a boat here, not the grim adjective the surface offers. A Saddleback is a British breed of pig, and the definition is one bare word at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: The Saddleback is a British breed of pig, black with a white band over the shoulders like a saddle.

indicators.note: 'In' says the answer is inside the words that follow, sitting there letter by letter in order.

parts.note: an unbroken run starting at the fourth letter of 'kitsch' and stopping three letters into 'leprechaun'

explanation.surface: A tacky leprechaun ornament being hauled in from somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: Schlep is Yiddish and long since at home in English: to schlep something is to lug it further than you want to. The word break between the two long words covers the join.
explanation.definitionFit: To schlep something is to haul it awkwardly from one place to another, which is what drag means.

definitions.meaning: first definition: something that takes no effort at all
second definition: the Christmas story acted out at school, a play performed by children

explanation.surface: A school Christmas production described as no trouble whatever to put on.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition asks you to stop hearing the idiom and hear two words: a nativity really is a children's play. The apostrophe goes unmarked, which is why (6,4) looks like two plain words.
explanation.definitionFit: Child's play is anything done without effort, and a nativity is literally a play put on by children.

clue.text: Ten in play, very small scene

indicators.note: 'In' puts what stands before it inside what stands after it, planting one set of letters within the other.

parts.note: a play staged in a theatre is a drama
ten in figures is 10, which on the page is a capital I beside an O

explanation.surface: Ten actors crowded into a play that has only a tiny stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ten' hands over letters rather than a Roman numeral: the digits 1 and 0 are read as the letters they resemble. A diorama is the modelled scene in a museum case, with its painted backdrop and tiny figures.
explanation.definitionFit: A diorama is a miniature scene built in three dimensions, a landscape or a tableau shrunk into a box.

indicators.note: Something changed is no longer as it was, so the letters come out in an arrangement other than the one given.

parts.note: anagram fodder, five letters

explanation.surface: A thorn on a branch that has grown round to point somewhere else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Changed direction' reads as one phrase and the last word is the definition standing alone. Short anagrams of ordinary nouns hide well, because the fodder reads as a thing rather than as raw letters.
explanation.definitionFit: North is one of the four points of the compass, so it is a direction.

indicators.note: Something written upwards runs against the usual direction, so the letters are read back to front.

parts.note: the face of a clock or a watch is its dial

explanation.surface: A playing card dealt onto the table with its face showing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Face upwards' is one picture in the surface and two instructions underneath: a word for face, then that word turned round. Placed and the answer are both past tenses, which is how the definition is checked.
explanation.definitionFit: To lay something somewhere is to place it there, and laid is the past form that matches 'placed'.

parts.note: the initial of mum with the possessive 's kept, M'S

indicators.note: the setter's bracketed note (inits) says the answer is made from initial letters

parts.note: initial letter of grub

explanation.surface: A flavour enhancer turns up in the food Mum cooks.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is an abbreviation, which is why the setter flags it with (inits): M and 'S from mum's, then G from grub. Read whole, the clue also describes the additive sitting in the family dinner.
explanation.definitionFit: Monosodium glutamate is a flavour enhancer added to processed and takeaway dishes.

clue.text: Type of train from Leeds I vandalised

indicators.note: Vandalising something leaves it wrecked and its parts strewn about, which is what happens to these letters.

parts.note: anagram fodder, six letters

explanation.surface: A service out of Leeds that vandals have got at.
explanation.walkthrough: Railway people call a locomotive a diesel, so a fuel answers 'type of train'. Leeds is a city in West Yorkshire with a busy mainline station, which lets the place name sit quietly in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A diesel is a locomotive driven by a diesel engine, the everyday word for a train that is not electric or steam.

indicators.note: oddly here means taking the odd-numbered letters, first, third and fifth, of the name

parts.note: a man's name, used here only for its letters

explanation.surface: A man called Duncan is said to carry an unusual genetic code.
explanation.walkthrough: The first, third and fifth letters of Duncan spell the answer; (inits) flags that it is an abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Deoxyribonucleic acid is the molecule carrying the hereditary instructions in living cells.

clue.text: Point to small exam as the most pleasant

parts.note: s = south, one of the points of the compass
wee is small, Scottish in origin and used across Britain
a test is an exam

explanation.surface: A teacher holding up a short exam as the nicest thing on the timetable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Point' opens the clue where a verb belongs and is a compass point, the commonest way a single letter is clued. Three separate pieces run together with only 'to' between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Sweet means pleasant or agreeable - a sweet nature, a sweet day - so the sweetest is the most pleasant.

indicators.note: not half says the first half of the word, five of its ten letters, is thrown away

explanation.surface: Someone asks if they should refocus and gets the slangy reply 'Not half!', meaning 'absolutely'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not half!' is British slang for 'very much so', but here it literally removes the front half of refocusing.
explanation.definitionFit: Using and employing both mean putting something to work for a purpose.

indicators.note: Rum is British for odd or peculiar, and letters called odd are not standing in their proper order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, seven letters

explanation.surface: An order at the bar: beer for nothing, and spirits for nobody.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word is a drink or an order about drink, and the last is the one doing crossword work: a rum do is a strange business. To unleash a dog is to let it off the lead.
explanation.definitionFit: To unleash something is to set it free - a dog, a storm, a torrent of abuse - and let it go where it will.

clue.text: Be at great length to have rightful place

parts.note: the verb taken as it stands
anything that goes on at great length is long

explanation.surface: Someone talking for hours in the hope of earning their place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Be at great length' reads as one instruction to a bore and splits after its first word. The definition is a phrase because the answer has no one-word synonym worth the name.
explanation.definitionFit: To belong somewhere is to have a rightful place there - the chair belongs in the kitchen, and so do you.

definitions.meaning: first definition: fenced spaces for keeping animals in
second definition: a pen is a female swan

explanation.surface: Wire runs and cages put up to keep poultry in.
explanation.walkthrough: The four words read as one straight description, and the question mark is the only warning that the last of them is a second definition. A male swan is a cob and the female a pen.
explanation.definitionFit: A pen is a fenced enclosure for animals; a pen is also a female swan, so 'birds' names the creatures rather than their housing.

definitions.meaning: first definition: a small silvery food fish of the salmon family
second definition: the past tense of smell

explanation.surface: A fish that has been out of the water rather too long.
explanation.walkthrough: Two words, two definitions, with nothing joining them but the temptation to read them as one complaint. British English keeps 'smelt' alongside 'smelled' as the past of smell.
explanation.definitionFit: A smelt is a small silvery fish sold for the table; and smelt is the past tense of smell, so whatever stank smelt.

parts.note: c = cold, the letter on a British tap
a rash is an outbreak on the skin

explanation.surface: An outbreak of colds that somebody set off without meaning to.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cold outbreak' reads as one piece of health news and is two pieces of wordplay: the letter from the tap, then the thing on the skin. A crash is an accident of cars or planes rather than any mishap.
explanation.definitionFit: A crash is a violent collision - two cars, a plane coming down - which is the kind of accident the word names.

clue.text: Chaotic ops eventually hold group of trees

indicators.note: To hold something is to keep it within you, so these words have the answer sitting whole inside them.

parts.note: an unbroken run from the last letter of 'Chaotic', through 'ops', to the first letter of 'eventually'

explanation.surface: Disorderly troops who finally take a stand of trees and keep it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chaotic' looks exactly like an anagram instruction standing in front of three loose letters, and it is part of the hiding place instead. Nothing here needs rearranging.
explanation.definitionFit: A copse is a small group of trees, a thicket smaller than a wood.

definitions.note: Swimming baths is the British name for a public swimming pool and keeps a plural form for a single building, so it answers a singular word.
definitions.meaning: first definition: the common fund everyone pays into
second definition: the water at a municipal swimming place

explanation.surface: A cat picking its way around the local swimming baths.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kitty' is a cat in the surface and money in the clue: the pot chipped into for a bet or an office round. Swimming baths is what a British town calls its public pool, sign and all.
explanation.definitionFit: A pool is money put into a common fund, which is what a kitty is; and the pool is the water you swim in at the baths.

clue.text: Ruin it all, not quite a sort of bliss?

parts.note: to mar something is to spoil or ruin it

indicators.note: not quite means the word all falls one letter short at its end

explanation.surface: A gloomy warning that something will spoil everything, set against the cliché of wedded happiness.
explanation.walkthrough: MAR and IT are followed by AL, which is all cut short. The definition works by completing the phrase 'marital bliss'.
explanation.definitionFit: Marital bliss is the stock phrase for happiness in marriage, so the adjective names a kind of bliss.

parts.note: Morse is the code of dots and dashes
l = left

explanation.surface: The last piece of a coded message still lying about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scrap of code' invites you to take three words as one phrase; only the first is the definition and 'of' is there to join it on. A morsel is a small piece, most often of food.
explanation.definitionFit: A morsel is a small piece broken off - a morsel of bread, a morsel of gossip - which is what a scrap is.

clue.text: Impudent troops on outskirts of Salisbury

parts.note: the SAS is the Special Air Service, the British Army's special forces regiment

indicators.note: The outskirts of a place are its outer edges, so only the outside letters of the word are wanted.

parts.note: the first and last letters of SALISBURY

explanation.surface: Soldiers camped on the edge of a quiet cathedral city.
explanation.walkthrough: Salisbury Plain, the open country beside that Wiltshire city, is where the British Army trains, so the soldiers and the place name sit together without a murmur. Sassy is cheek with some style to it.
explanation.definitionFit: Sassy means cheeky and bold in a lively way, the American cousin of 'saucy' and a fair match for impudent.
